item.text: {"reviews":[{"benchmark":"arc","instrument_review":"ARC-AGI-2 supports comparisons of performance on unfamiliar grid puzzles when exposure, settings, spending limits and benchmark revisions are comparable. Its examples make the task understandable, and exact grid matching gives a clear scoring rule. Human testing and checks for repeated solution rules support puzzle selection, but the human results cover a larger pool than the final benchmark. Matching sets for human difficulty does not establish equal difficulty for AI systems. The reported score needs careful interpretation: the software averages the fraction of new inputs solved within each problem, whereas the dataset reserves “fully solved” for problems with every input correct. Verified evaluations use one run, and the supplied materials do not establish how stable scores or close rankings are. Public materials and revision records aid inspection, although public exposure and corrections complicate comparisons. Scores provide evidence about these grid tasks; broader claims about reasoning or intelligence remain unresolved by the supplied studies.","supported_claims":["The task tests producing new grid outputs from worked examples, with exact size and colour required for credit.","Puzzle construction included human solving sessions and developer checks for repeated rules, providing evidence of deliberate selection.","Verified evaluations specify settings and spending limits, supporting comparisons within those conditions.","Public puzzles, scoring software, marking tests and dated changes make important parts of the evaluation inspectable."],"documented_problems":["The software’s fractional problem scores differ from the dataset’s definition of a fully solved problem, creating a reporting ambiguity.","Corrections to squares and unclear examples changed benchmark materials, but affected AI scores are not all recalculated.","Public evaluation puzzles can be seen by anyone, and the hidden-test policy acknowledges that information could escape.","Verified testing uses a single run, so each reported result represents that run rather than an average across repetitions."],"missing_information":["Repeat-run estimates or ranges are absent, leaving the size of ordinary score fluctuations unknown.","No systematic study establishes the effects of changing instructions, grid presentation or software.","The supplied evidence does not establish that alternative routes to high scores have all been excluded.","No supplied study connects scores to success in language, social interaction or real-world work.","The preparer did not independently test the entire marking system or inspect the complete reporting archive."],"reinterpretations":["Read the overall score as an average of within-problem input success fractions, not simply the percentage of problems fully solved.","Treat matched human difficulty as evidence about human performance, not proof of equivalent AI test sets or stable AI scores.","Interpret a high score as successful grid-task performance under stated conditions; it does not establish which reasoning process produced it.","Compare results with attention to exposure, evaluation route, settings and revisions; keep ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 distinct."],"closing_note":"The main instruction ambiguity is the meaning of “solved”: reporting should distinguish a correct input, a fully solved problem and the software’s averaged score. The review instructions themselves are clear."},{"benchmark":"designqa","instrument_review":"DesignQA offers a useful examination of finding and applying rules and interpreting vehicle materials within the supplied Formula SAE setting. Real rules, designs and practitioner contributions support its practical relevance, but one rulebook and limited task types cannot establish broad engineering competence. Its six groups expose different aspects of performance, yet their sizes and marking methods differ substantially. Equal weighting makes the overall score sensitive to small groups, and the supplied evidence does not establish a common skill measured by that number. Wording-sensitive marking can also penalize answers for reasons beyond engineering understanding. Comparisons require particular care because systems receive different information supplies, and the reported variation does not establish stability under identical repeated conditions. Public materials permit partial inspection, but incomplete historical records limit reproduction. Results are most defensible as performance on these particular tasks with the stated inputs and scoring methods.","supported_claims":["Questions use actual competition rules, vehicle designs and test data, giving the tasks a concrete connection to engineering work.","The six groups cover rule retrieval, terminology, component identification, dimensions and performance checks.","Additional reviewers checked manually written questions, although the coverage and depth of checking had exceptions.","Experiments changing passages and visual information show attention to how supplied information affects performance.","Public questions, instructions, scoring code and some responses allow inspection of parts of the evaluation."],"documented_problems":["Marking can depend on wording and formatting; examples include missing commas and valid related rules omitted from reference answers.","Group sizes range from 1,192 rule-finding questions to 16 performance questions, while the overall score weights groups equally.","Systems receive either whole rulebooks or retrieved passages, so comparisons combine model performance with information supply.","All described scale-bar drawings comply with the rule, allowing an always-yes response to earn the decision credit on that portion.","The released materials do not fully link historical software, settings and inputs to every result, and one answer file has fewer rows than the paper’s corresponding question count."],"missing_information":["Reviewer disagreement rates, remaining answer errors and a complete study of marking accuracy and consistency are not established.","Identical-condition repeat results and sufficient uncertainty information for judging small ranking differences are absent.","No human-engineer baseline is reported.","A protected test set, systematic exposure check and clear training and repeated-submission rules were not established.","The inspected materials lack a clear record of revisions’ score effects, a licence file and complete reuse rules; closely ranked results need stronger support.","Treat the always-yes opportunity as a demonstrated scoring shortcut, not evidence that any tested AI used it.","The five passage-set trials show sensitivity to changed inputs, not repeatability with an identical test."],"closing_note":"The supplied description leaves acceptable answer wording and the boundaries for training on released questions or repeatedly submitting results insufficiently clear.
